meta.title: Who really said "Show me a sane man and I will cure him for you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Carl Jung never published it. The line survives only as a second-hand recollection printed in 1975, and older versions credited Freud. What the record shows.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Show me a sane man and I will cure him for you'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in Jung's writings: the quote reaches print only in 1975, via a colleague's memory. Earlier versions were credited to Freud and an unnamed pupil.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist, founder of analytical psychology
answer.sourceLine: Jung never published this line. The only evidence is second-hand: his associate Jolande Jacobi told biographer Vincent Brome in 1963 that Jung had said “Show me a sane person and I’ll cure him for you,” and Brome printed the familiar wording in The Guardian on 19 July 1975 — after Jung’s death. Quote Investigator ↗ judges that Jung probably made a remark of this type, but no primary source in Jung’s own hand or voice has been found.

source.heading: Where the words actually appear

source.excerpt: Show me a sane man and I will cure him for you.
trail: 1957 — the Freudian ancestor. Robin A. Hodgkin’s Education and Change quotes a female pupil of Freud, unnamed: “Show me a normal man and I will cure him,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
1963 — the recollection. Biographer Vincent Brome interviewed Jung’s long-time associate Jolande Jacobi ↗, who attributed to Jung the words “Show me a sane person and I’ll cure him for you.”

1975 — into print. Quote Investigator’s earliest located instance of the familiar wording is Brome’s article “The man who woke the world” in The Guardian, 19 July 1975, page 9; that March the British Medical Journal had run a Freud-credited variant.

1978 onward — canonised. Brome’s biography Jung (Atheneum, 1978 ↗) carries the quote at page 200 with the Jacobi footnote; Robert Byrne’s 1984 quotation compilation then fixed it to “C. G. Jung” for the aggregator era.
source.excerptNote: The form Jacobi gave Brome differs: “Show me a sane person and I’ll cure him for you.” Both wordings are documented by Quote Investigator ↗; neither has been found in anything Jung himself wrote.

source.rightsNote: Jung died in 1961, but this line is not tied to any work he published. The documents that actually carry it are modern: Vincent Brome’s Guardian article of 19 July 1975 and his biography Jung (Atheneum, 1978), both first published well after 1930 and both still in copyright. Treat the wording as coming from an in-copyright modern source, not from a public-domain work of Jung’s.

author.name: Carl Jung
author.heading: Who was Carl Jung?
author.metaLine: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist & founder of analytical psychology
author.bio: Carl Gustav Jung (26 July 1875 – 6 June 1961) was a Swiss psychiatrist, psychotherapist and psychologist who founded the school of analytical psychology. He gave the language the archetype, the collective unconscious, introversion and extraversion, and individuation. He was also, by the testimony of those around him, a witty and deliberately provocative talker — which is precisely why aphorisms he never wrote down keep attaching themselves to his name.

misattribution.heading: How the line travelled
misattribution.intro: This is a quotation with two problems: the wording drifted, and the name attached to it changed at least twice before it settled on Jung.

items.who: An unnamed female pupil of Freud
items.why: Robin A. Hodgkin’s Education and Change (1957) credits “one of Freud’s pupils” with “Show me a normal man and I will cure him.” Quote Investigator ↗ notes her identity is still unknown.
In March 1975 the British Medical Journal printed “Show me the normal man and I will cure him” and gave it to Freud — while noting it “may or may not be apocryphal,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Carl Jung, in two different forms
items.why: What Jacobi reported to Brome was “Show me a sane person and I’ll cure him for you.” The now-standard “sane man … I will cure him for you” is the form Brome used in his 1975 Guardian article, as documented here ↗.

Quotation sites repeat an Observer source line — for example this aggregator entry ↗. Quote Investigator’s citation for that same date is The Guardian’s Saturday Page, Vincent Brome’s article “The man who woke the world,” page 9.
Mainstream aggregators carry the line with no citation at all — The Quotations Page ↗ files it under user-contributed quotations with nothing but “Carl Jung, Swiss psychologist.”

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: Jung probably said something like it in conversation, but the words reach us only through a colleague’s memory recorded after his death — and near-identical sayings were credited to Freud and to an unnamed analyst years earlier, as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Jung
lead: The line works because it compresses something Jung genuinely argued. In a 1932 article on Freud’s historical setting he dismissed the idea of “a normal man” as a strange fiction — the notion that anyone is textbook-healthy was, to him, the illusion worth treating. The aphorism is the joke version of that position, and it is entirely in character.

But character is not evidence. What we actually have is a colleague’s memory of a witticism, recorded after the man was dead, and a family of near-identical sayings that were already circulating in Freudian circles before anyone put Jung’s name to them.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s earliest relevant citation is not about Jung at all: Robin A. Hodgkin’s Education and Change (1957) credits “one of Freud’s pupils,” a female psychoanalyst who is never named, with “Show me a normal man and I will cure him.” Her identity remains unknown.

In March 1975 the British Medical Journal printed “Show me the normal man and I will cure him” and gave it to Freud, while conceding it may or may not be apocryphal. The Jung-credited wording surfaced in print four months later.
context.pull: A remark that sounds exactly like Jung is still not a remark documented in Jung.
